intro: “Just”, “already” and “yet” are mostly used with the present perfect to show how an action relates to now. They are essential when you check what is done and what is not done yet.
objectifs: Say that something happened a very short time ago with “have just + past participle”.
Use already in positive sentences and yet in negatives and questions.
Put each word in the right place in the sentence.
Know the American use with the past simple and the meaning of “still haven't”.

sections.titre: Just: a very short time ago
texte: “Just” shows that an action happened a very short time ago. It goes between have / has and the past participle.
The news is fresh, and the result is often important now.
exemples: She isn't here now — you missed her.
The bus has just arrived. Let's run!

texte: “Already” shows that an action is finished, often sooner than expected. In positive sentences it goes between have / has and the past participle; it can also go at the end for emphasis.
In a question, “already” shows surprise: “Have you already finished?” (That was quick!).
exemples: It's done; you don't need to pay.
We don't want to see it again.
Have you already eaten? It's only eleven!

texte: “Yet” goes at the end of the sentence. In a question, it asks if something expected has happened. In a negative, it means the action has not happened, but we expect it to happen.
We do not use it in simple positive sentences with this meaning. A typical short answer is “Not yet.”

lignes: Have you done your homework yet?
Is it done? I expect it.
Not done, but I will do it.

texte: Just and already: between the helper verb and the past participle (middle of the sentence). Yet: at the end of the sentence.
“Still” can be added to show impatience: “I still haven't received my visa” (I expected it before now). It goes before haven't / hasn't.

In American English, people very often use the past simple with just, already and yet: “I just ate”, “Did you eat yet?”, “I already told him”. This is correct in the USA and in English-speaking Canada.
In British English, the present perfect is still the norm: “I've just eaten”, “Have you eaten yet?”. This site uses the British form, but you should understand both.
exemples: Present perfect with just — same meaning.

formule: have / has + just / already + past participle · haven't + past participle … yet · Have … + past participle … yet?
prononciation: “just” is /dʒʌst/: j as in “jean”, u as in “cup”. Before a consonant, the final t often disappears: I've just seen /aɪv dʒʌs ˈsiːn/.
“already” is /ɔːlˈredi/: stress on the second syllable.
“yet” is /jet/, with the y sound of “yes”. Do not say “jet” /dʒet/.
“Not yet” has a falling tone, often with the stress on yet: not YET.
erreurs: I come from finishing my work.
For a very recent action: have just + past participle.
already goes between have and the participle (or at the end).
yet usually goes at the end (the middle position is very formal).
Have you already seen him yesterday?

dialogue.contexte: The day before moving house in Lyon, Awa and her partner Hugo check their to-do list.
lignes: Have you called the moving company yet?
Yes, I've just called them. They're coming at eight tomorrow.
Great. I've already packed the kitchen.
Already? That was fast! Have you packed the books yet?
No, not yet. I haven't found enough boxes.
I've just bought ten more. They're in the car.
Recent action with a result now.
Perfect. Oh, and we still haven't told the bank our new address.
Don't worry, I'll do it online tonight.

mots: before now, or sooner than expected
continuing until now, often longer than expected
to put things in a bag or box
to get something that someone sends you
Have you sent the invoice yet?
to make something go to another person (send – sent – sent)
They haven't delivered the parcel yet.
to take something to a person or place
I've already done three tasks today.
a piece of work you must do

exercices.consigne: Complete with just, already or yet.
items: I've ___ eaten, thanks. I'm not hungry.
She's ___ gone out. You missed her by one minute.
The film has ___ started — sit down quickly!

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the word in brackets in the right place.
items: We still haven't received the results.

exercices.consigne: Write a present perfect sentence with the word given (✓ = done, ✗ = not done).
items: I haven't cleaned the flat yet.
call the doctor ✓ two minutes ago (just)
Have you paid the rent yet?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Have you already met him last week?
Did you meet him last week?

exercices.consigne: Rewrite these American English sentences in British English (present perfect).
items: Did you book the tickets yet?
Have you booked the tickets yet?

exercices.consigne: Check your day or week in five sentences with just, already, yet and still.
items: It's Thursday evening. I've already finished my big project at work. I've just cooked dinner for my family. I haven't called my mother yet — I'll do it after dinner. And I still haven't started the book my friend gave me!

a_retenir: have just + past participle = a very short time ago (I've just arrived).
already (sooner than expected): between have and the participle, in positive sentences.
yet at the end: questions and negatives; Not yet.
still + haven't = not yet, and I'm impatient.
American English often uses the past simple (I just ate, Did you eat yet?).
